What the official sources say

  • SC Code 15-67-210: occupation of premises by another is deemed in subordination to the legal title unless the premises were held and possessed adversely to the legal title for ten years before the action commenced. (S.C. Code 15-67-210; source)
  • SC Code 15-67-220 (color of title): an occupant who entered under claim of title founded on a written instrument as a conveyance, or on a court decree or judgment, with continued occupation for ten years, is deemed to have held adversely; possession of one lot is not possession of another lot of the same tract. (S.C. Code 15-67-220; source)
  • SC Code 15-67-250: for adverse possession not founded on a written instrument or judgment, land is deemed possessed only in the listed cases; a tenant's possession is deemed the landlord's possession until ten years from termination of the tenancy (or from refusal to pay rent if no written lease). (S.C. Code 15-67-250; source)
  • SC Code 27-40-430 (landlord remedy): the landlord may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and may recover damages provided in 27-40-760(c). (S.C. Code 27-40 (section number as shown in excerpt, text preceding 27-40-440); source)

South Carolina Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my South Carolina house?

Check the statute and talk to a South Carolina attorney about your facts.

How many years must someone occupy South Carolina land to claim it by adverse possession?

Ten years. Under S.C. Code 15-67-210, a person who occupies land is presumed to hold it under the legal owner's title unless the land was held and possessed against that title for ten years before the lawsuit began.

The same section presumes that the holder of record title has been in possession as the law requires. That presumption is the starting point in every South Carolina squatter dispute. The person making the claim has to overcome it, and the owner does not have to prove anything until the claimant does.

A stranger who walks into a house last month is a trespasser, and a different set of tools applies, covered below.

What does a claimant have to prove?

A claimant must show possession that was actual, open, notorious, hostile, continuous and exclusive for the whole statutory period. The South Carolina Court of Appeals used those words in Butler v. Lindsey (1987), which also states that the claimant must show the extent of the possession.

The burden rests on the person relying on adverse possession. Because possession is presumed to follow legal title, the proof must be by clear and convincing evidence. That is a higher bar than the ordinary civil standard.

  • Actual: the person physically uses the land, not merely claims it on paper.
  • Open and notorious: the use is visible enough that a reasonably attentive owner would know about it.
  • Hostile: the occupant does not have the owner's permission.
  • Continuous and exclusive: no long gaps, and no sharing the land with the owner.

Permission matters here. A relative who stays rent-free with the owner's blessing is not in hostile possession.

How do deeds, court judgments and fences change the claim?

They change what counts as possession and how much land a claimant can reach. South Carolina treats a claim backed by a written conveyance or court decree differently from a claim with no paper at all.

Under 15-67-220, an occupant who claims under a written instrument or judgment and continuously occupies part of the land it describes for ten years is treated as holding adversely. Section 15-67-230 lists what counts as possession in that situation: land that is usually cultivated or improved, land protected by a substantial enclosure, land used for fuel, fencing timber or ordinary use, and the uncleared part of a partly improved farm or lot. Where land is divided into lots, possession of one lot is not possession of another lot in the same tract.

The rule is tighter for a claim without any writing. Section 15-67-240 limits the claim to land actually occupied, and no other. Section 15-67-250 requires that the land be both protected by a substantial enclosure and usually cultivated or improved.

A squatter with no paper must show real, physical use of the specific ground claimed.

Can a tenant become an owner by staying put?

Generally no. Section 15-67-260 treats a tenant's possession as the landlord's possession until ten years after the tenancy ends, or ten years from the tenant's refusal to pay rent when there is no written lease.

The tenancy has to end first, and a landlord who lets years pass after a termination without court action takes a risk.

Which South Carolina removal process fits which situation?

It depends on whether the occupant ever had a lease or the owner's consent. The table summarizes the three statutory routes found in Title 15 and Title 27.

SituationStatuteWhere filedKey timing
Tenant who stopped paying or whose term endedS.C. Code 27-37-10 and followingMagistrateTen days after service to show cause; writ within five days of a verdict; 24 hours to vacate after the writ is presented
Person who entered without consent or warrant of lawS.C. Code 15-67-610 to 15-67-640MagistrateNotice to quit; warrant if the person has not left within five days of personal service
Unlawful occupant of a residential dwelling who is not a tenant, guest or family memberS.C. Code 27-37-200 to 27-37-350 (effective June 30, 2026)Clerk of court or chief magistrateEx parte order on good cause; hearing within 24 hours of filing unless delay is shown to be justified

What is the 2026 process for removing unlawful occupants of a dwelling?

It is a new article of Title 27, Chapter 37, effective June 30, 2026 under 2026 Act No. 252 (H.3387), that lets the owner or the owner's representative file a verified petition to remove someone who has no legal right to be in a residential dwelling. The text is on the S.C. Statehouse site.

An unlawful occupant under that article is someone who occupies without the owner's permission, has no legal right to occupy under state law and has no tenant protections. A representative can be an authorized agent, or the personal representative of an estate in probate.

The petition is filed with the clerk of court or chief magistrate of the county where the property sits, and the filing fee matches a Court of Common Pleas filing. The petition must allege several items, including that:

  • the filer is the owner or the owner's representative;
  • the occupants entered and stay without permission and are not guests;
  • the owner told them to leave and they refused;
  • the home was never leased to them and they are not current or former tenants;
  • they are not immediate family members;
  • no litigation is pending between the owner and the occupants over the property.

If good cause is shown, the court can issue an ex parte order that takes effect when entered, and a hearing is held within 24 hours of filing unless good cause supports a delay. After a hearing the court may exclude the occupants permanently and order them to pay repair, service and court costs. Violating the order is a felony with up to three years in prison, a fine of up to $3,000, or both. The article also lets a wrongfully removed person sue for restored possession, actual damages and $1,000 in statutory damages, so owners should use it only where the facts fit.

What is the older trespasser process in Title 15?

Sections 15-67-610 to 15-67-640 let an owner ask a magistrate to serve a notice to quit on someone who entered or occupies land without consent or warrant of law. If the occupant does not leave within five days after personal service, the magistrate may issue a warrant, and a sheriff or constable ejects the person using necessary force.

An occupant can block the warrant by appearing within the five days, showing a bona fide color of claim to possession and posting a bond with approved security. Either side may appeal, and the magistrate cannot issue the warrant until five days after announcing the decision.

Why can't a South Carolina landlord change the locks or cut utilities?

Because S.C. Code 27-40-760 bars a landlord from recovering possession of a dwelling unit by action or otherwise except in the situations the chapter allows, and that includes willfully cutting off essential services. Section 27-40-660 gives the tenant a remedy when a landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant: possession back or an ended lease, plus the greater of three months' rent or twice actual damages, and attorney's fees.

Under 27-40-710, rent is late if unpaid within five days of the due date, and other breaches end the lease if not fixed within fourteen days of written notice.

When is it a crime to enter or stay on someone's property in South Carolina?

Entering after notice is a misdemeanor. Section 16-11-600 covers entry after the owner or tenant has posted notice in four conspicuous places on the borders of the land or marked it with visible purple paint, and carries a fine of up to $100, up to 30 days in jail, or both. Section 16-11-620 covers entering a dwelling or other premises after a warning, or refusing to leave when ordered without good cause, with a fine of up to $200 or up to 30 days.

What can you do with a house that has an occupant you cannot remove yet?

Sell it as-is, with the occupant issue disclosed, to a buyer who is willing to take that on. Some buyers want the property delivered vacant, so ask early what a buyer expects.

  • Gather the deed, any probate papers, tax bills and proof you were paying them.
  • Write down when you last visited and what you saw, because dates matter in any ten-year question.
  • Keep any text or letter showing you told the occupant to leave.
  • Check with a South Carolina attorney before starting a court case or signing a contract.

We buy South Carolina houses as-is, including inherited homes and houses with tenant problems. Tell us what is going on and we will say plainly whether we can work with it.

More questions about South Carolina Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Can a squatter take my South Carolina house after ten years?

Only if the squatter proves possession that was actual, open, notorious, hostile, continuous and exclusive for ten years, by clear and convincing evidence. South Carolina presumes the record owner has possession, so the claimant carries the burden. A lawyer should review your facts.

Does paying property tax matter in a South Carolina adverse possession claim?

The sections of Chapter 67 that we read do not make tax payment an element of the claim. Tax records still help an owner show who treated the land as theirs, so keep your bills and receipts.

How fast can I remove an unlawful occupant under the 2026 law?

The statute allows an immediate ex parte order on a showing of good cause and a hearing within 24 hours of filing unless good cause supports delay. It sets no fixed removal deadline, so the timing of the actual removal depends on the court and the enforcement official.

Can I sell my South Carolina house while someone is living in it without permission?

Yes, you can sell, but you must disclose the situation and the buyer decides whether to proceed. Many buyers wait until the home is vacant, while some investors will buy as-is. Ask a South Carolina attorney about the title and contract wording first.

What law governs landlords and tenants in South Carolina?

The South Carolina Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Chapter 40 of Title 27, covers most residential rentals. It sets what a lease must say, what the landlord must repair, how deposits work and how a tenancy ends.

Section 27-40-20 directs that the Act be liberally construed to promote its purposes, and 27-40-60 allows a good-faith dispute to be settled by agreement. The full text sits on the Legislature's Chapter 40 page. For an owner thinking of selling a rental, the Act answers a practical question: what do I still owe this tenant after the closing?

What must a landlord disclose and repair?

A landlord must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner (27-40-420). The duty to repair is broad. Section 27-40-440 requires the landlord to make repairs and do what is reasonably necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable.

  • The disclosure stays current and can be enforced against a successor landlord, owner or manager (27-40-420(b)).
  • Habitability covers code compliance, running water, reasonable hot water and heat, and working electrical, plumbing and heating.
  • A tenant who has a material breach by the landlord can end the lease after written notice if it is not fixed within 14 days (27-40-610).

For a house that needs work, this matters when you sell. A buyer inheriting a tenant also inherits the repair duty, and pending complaints tend to surface in negotiations.

How do security deposits work?

On termination the landlord returns the deposit less amounts withheld for rent and damages, and sends an itemized written notice within thirty days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it, whichever is later (27-40-410(a)).

A landlord who misses that step can face recovery of three times the wrongfully withheld amount plus attorney's fees. The Act sets no cap on the deposit amount, according to the definitions in 27-40-210.

When a rental changes hands, 27-40-410(e) and 27-40-450 govern who holds the money. The person holding the landlord's interest at termination is bound by the deposit rules, and a seller who conveys in good faith is relieved after written notice to the tenant, but remains liable for the deposit unless it is transferred and the tenant is notified. Put the deposit transfer on the closing checklist in writing.

What are a tenant's rights on entry, privacy and retaliation?

The landlord needs 24 hours notice before entering, at reasonable times, except in an emergency (27-40-530(c)). Scheduled periodic services may occur between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., and tenant-requested services between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m., with an announcement beforehand.

Retaliation is prohibited. A landlord cannot raise rent above fair market value, cut essential services or bring a possession action because a tenant complained to a code enforcement agency or to the landlord. Remedies run up to three months rent or treble damages (27-40-910). A tenant raising the defense against a rule to vacate must notify the landlord in writing within ten days of service.

TopicRuleSection
Deposit itemization30 days after termination and demand27-40-410(a)
Entry notice24 hours, except emergencies27-40-530(c)
Landlord breach cure period14 days after written notice27-40-610
Retaliation defense notice10 days after service27-40-910
Month-to-month ending30 days written notice27-40-770(b)

How can a tenancy be ended?

A month-to-month tenancy ends with at least thirty days of written notice from either side, and a week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven (27-40-770). A fixed-term lease generally runs to its end date unless a breach lets one side terminate earlier.

  • Unpaid rent: if the tenant fails to pay within five days from the due date after written notice, the landlord may terminate (27-40-710(B)).
  • Other breach: termination not less than 14 days after receipt of notice if the tenant does not remedy it (27-40-710(A)).
  • Abandonment: an unexplained absence for 15 days after a rent default may be treated as abandonment (27-40-730).

A landlord may not use lockouts or cut services to recover possession (27-40-760). Court is the route, and our eviction process guide walks through the magistrate steps in 27-37.

What happens to the lease when a rental house is sold?

The statutes give you notice and deposit duties to handle, and they do not by themselves end the tenancy. Whether a buyer takes subject to the lease depends on the lease terms and the buyer's deal, so have an attorney review the specifics.

Collect these before you talk to any buyer:

  • The signed lease with every addendum, plus the current rent ledger.
  • The deposit amount and where it is held.
  • A record of repair requests and your responses, since habitability disputes carry over in practice.
  • Written notice to the tenant of the new owner and contact details, as 27-40-420 and 27-40-450 contemplate.

If the tenant is behind or the house is in poor shape, some owners sell as-is for cash and let the buyer handle the tenancy decision. That is a business choice to weigh against selling vacant.

What costs should a South Carolina rental owner expect at sale?

Expect property tax proration and a deed recording fee. Real estate taxes are due between September 30 and January 15, and the penalty rises 3 percent after January 15, then 7 and 5 percent after February 2 and March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

The recording fee is $1.85 per $500 of value, with $1.30 to the state and $0.55 to the county, and the grantor generally pays it (12-24-10 and 12-24-20). A rented house is assessed at 6 percent as other real property, while an owner-occupied legal residence gets 4 percent only if it is not rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year (12-43-220).

How is rent set, and what if a lease has no term?

Rent is payable at the start of each month, or at the start of any term of one month or less, and it can be apportioned day to day unless the parties agree otherwise. When no term is fixed, the tenancy is month to month (27-40-310).

That day-to-day proration helps at a closing, since rent for the part of a month after the sale date can be divided on the settlement statement. A landlord also cannot enforce an unperfected contractual lien on a tenant's household goods (27-40-740).

What happens when a tenant breaks a health or safety rule?

The landlord may enter and do the work after 14 days written notice, or sooner in an emergency, or terminate the lease if the tenant fails to comply (27-40-720). A tenant can raise maintenance defenses and counterclaims in a possession or rent case under 27-40-640, though certain defenses are waived if the landlord lacked notice 14 days before rent was due.

Left behind property worth $500 or less may be disposed of after abandonment under 27-40-730, while the landlord is liable above that figure only if grossly negligent. Keep photographs and dates, since a buyer's lender or inspector may ask for them.

More questions about South Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in South Carolina?

Thirty days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered, or after the tenant demands it, whichever is later. A landlord who fails to send the itemized notice and money can owe three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees (27-40-410).

Is there a cap on security deposits?

The Act's definitions in 27-40-210 set no cap or amount limit. Check your lease for the agreed amount.

Can a landlord enter without notice?

Only in an emergency. Otherwise 24 hours notice and reasonable times apply under 27-40-530.

Can a tenant withhold rent for repairs?

Section 27-40-640 does not create a general right to withhold rent. It lets a tenant raise defenses and counterclaims in a possession or rent action, and some maintenance defenses are waived if the landlord lacked timely notice.

What if a landlord retaliates after a complaint?

Retaliation is barred, and a landlord can owe up to three months rent or treble actual damages plus fees under 27-40-910. The tenant must give written notice of the defense within ten days after service of a rule to vacate.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in South Carolina?
We buy South Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What eviction notices does South Carolina require?

South Carolina lets a landlord end a residential tenancy only after the right written notice, and the number of days depends on the reason. The main rules sit in Title 27, Chapter 40 of the South Carolina Code, with the court process in Chapter 37.

SituationNotice or waitSection
Rent unpaid5 days after the due date, plus written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate27-40-710(B)
Other lease breachWritten notice; ends at least 14 days after receipt if not fixed in 14 days27-40-710(A)
Health and safety violation14 days after written notice, or promptly in an emergency27-40-720
Month-to-month tenancy30 days written notice27-40-770(b)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days written notice27-40-770(a)

How does the five-day nonpayment notice work?

If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant does not pay within five days of the due date, the landlord may terminate after giving written notice of the nonpayment and the intent to terminate. One notice for a lease term satisfies the requirement, and so does conspicuous language in the written lease.

When the lease contains that language, no separate notice is needed to begin an eviction, even after the original term expires for a month-to-month tenancy. The ejectment chapter adds that, for a residential lease, the five-day period counts as legal notice only if the written agreement states it in bold, conspicuous type.

The landlord may recover actual damages and seek injunctive relief, judgments or evictions in magistrate or circuit court without posting bond. Attorney's fees are available only if the landlord is represented by an attorney and the nonpayment was not in good faith.

What about a lease violation that is not about rent?

For a tenant breach other than nonpayment, the landlord delivers written notice that names the breaches, and the agreement terminates at least 14 days after the tenant receives it if the breach is not remedied within 14 days. A tenant who fixes the breach before the date in the notice stops the termination.

If a remedy cannot be finished in 14 days, the tenant avoids termination by starting it within that period and pursuing it in good faith. Health and safety violations under Section 27-40-720 follow a similar 14-day path, and the landlord may also enter to do repairs and bill the tenant when the problem can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning.

  • Put the specific breach in writing
  • Keep proof of the date the tenant received the notice
  • Note any repair the tenant starts within the 14 days
  • Do not change locks or cut utilities, because Section 27-40-760 bars recovering possession by action or otherwise except in listed cases

What happens in magistrate court after the notice period?

The landlord files in magistrate court, and the magistrate issues a written rule that tells the tenant to vacate or show cause why they should not be ejected. The tenant has ten days after service to respond.

If the tenant does not appear and show cause within ten days, the magistrate issues a warrant of ejectment carried out by a constable or the sheriff. If the tenant contests, the case is heard like any civil case and either party may demand a jury.

  • Landlord wins: within five days the magistrate issues a writ of ejectment.
  • Tenant wins: the tenant stays in possession until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, rent goes unpaid or another proceeding ejects them.
  • Appeal: an appeal does not stop the ejectment unless the tenant posts an appeal bond set by the magistrate, and the appeal is dismissed if the bond is not filed within five days after the notice of appeal is served.

The statute sets no day count for the hearing itself, so ask the magistrate's office in your county for current scheduling.

How is service handled when the tenant is hard to find?

The rule to show cause can be served by the usual summons methods, and the statute gives backup methods when no one answers. After two failed attempts at least 48 hours apart, at times at least eight hours apart, it may be affixed to the premises with documentation and mailed.

Mailing counts as service ten days after it is sent, and the ten-day show-cause period starts on the eleventh day. If the premises have been abandoned for 15 days or more before service, the rule may be posted on the most conspicuous part of the premises.

Related abandonment rules say an unexplained absence of 15 days after a rent default is treated as abandonment. If the tenant voluntarily ended the utilities, abandonment is immediate.

What happens when the sheriff carries out the writ?

The officer presents the writ and gives the occupants 24 hours to leave voluntarily. If they refuse, a deputy sheriff, though not a constable, may force entry using the least destructive means.

If the home appears occupied and no one answers, a copy of the writ is posted on the door or another conspicuous place, and after 24 hours a deputy may force entry. The officer may delay dispossession of ill or elderly tenants.

The eviction notice must tell the tenant that property placed on a public street may be removed by officials after 48 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. For property left behind after abandonment, a landlord may dispose of property worth $500 or less; anything above that must be handled under Sections 27-37-10 to 27-37-150.

Can a landlord retaliate or use self-help?

No. A landlord may not recover possession through self-help, including interrupting essential services, except in cases of abandonment, surrender or termination or as the chapter permits.

Section 27-40-910 also bars retaliation. After a tenant complains to a housing code agency or to the landlord about a violation of the chapter, the landlord may not raise rent above fair market value, cut essential services or bring a possession action, subject to listed exceptions.

A wrongfully dispossessed tenant may sue the landlord for damages under Section 27-37-140. Rent keeps accruing at the prior rate while the tenant remains after proceedings begin, and accepting rent does not waive the right to eject.

Can you sell a house with a tenant who is being evicted?

Yes, you can sell a rental while an eviction is pending, but the notice, the court case and the tenant's rights do not disappear at closing. A landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for later events after written notice to the tenant.

The landlord stays liable for the security deposit unless it is transferred and the tenant is notified in writing. A holdover tenant can also cost money: if the stay is a wilful violation, the landlord may recover up to three months of periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

  • Occupied house with a notice already served
  • Tenant who stopped paying months ago
  • Landlord who wants out before a court date
  • Heirs who inherited a rental with a lease

We buy houses as-is, including with tenants in place, so you may not have to finish the eviction first. Tell us where the notice or case stands when you call, and keep every notice, receipt and court paper for the closing.

More questions about South Carolina Eviction Notice Rules

How many days is a South Carolina eviction notice for nonpayment?

Five days after the rent due date, followed by written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate, or conspicuous language in the written lease. One notice for a lease term satisfies the requirement.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in South Carolina?

Thirty days of written notice, given before the termination date stated. Week-to-week tenancies need seven days, under Section 27-40-770.

How long does the tenant have to respond to the court?

Ten days after service of the rule to show cause. If the tenant does not show cause, the magistrate issues a warrant of ejectment.

Can a landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Section 27-40-760 bars recovering possession by action or otherwise, including by interrupting essential services, except in cases of abandonment, surrender or termination or as the chapter permits.

Does selling the house end the lease?

Not by itself. A landlord who conveys the property in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of later liability after written notice to the tenant, but remains liable for the deposit unless it is transferred and the tenant is told.
